pros: Linear time O(d·(n+b)) — can be O(n) for fixed-width keys
No comparisons at all — bypasses Ω(n log n) lower bound
Excellent for sorting integers, IP addresses, strings, and fixed-width data
Stable sort — essential for multi-key sorting and database operations
Predictable performance — independent of input data distribution
Dominates GPU sorting — highly parallelizable on SIMD architectures
Can be faster than Quick Sort for large n with fixed-width keys
Outer loop is simple and regular (good for hardware implementation)
MSD variant can terminate early for well-separated data
Optimal for sorting strings and variable-length keys (MSD version)
Cache-friendly when base is chosen appropriately (b ≈ cache line size)
cons: Requires O(n + b) auxiliary space (not in-place)
Performance depends heavily on choice of base b
Inefficient for small arrays (overhead of multiple passes)
Only works for discrete keys with positional representation
Requires keys to be decomposable into digits (not general objects)
Fixed overhead of b buckets even if many are empty
LSD version must process all digits even for small numbers
MSD version is complex to implement correctly (recursive, boundary cases)
Less cache-friendly than Quick Sort for certain access patterns
Floating-point numbers require special bit-level handling
Negative numbers need special treatment (biased representation)
Integer overhead in languages like Python can negate performance gains
